Yes, it’s a day to be surrounded by those you love, even if some topics may be taboo at the dinner table. But what’s love without conflict? Hyperallergic is not one to appease those who deserve a light ribbing, particularly in an art world that prides itself on being so cutting-edge and consequential — for better or worse.

So, we’ve chosen to whet your appetites a little before your big meal by roasting our dear art community and reminding us all that laughter and humor are integral to how we digest the world and its many foibles and maddening realities.

The Museum of Modern Art’s refusal to let go of its billionaire trustee is the saddest, yet least surprising thing ever. A museum birthed and continually fed by the ultra-rich and their scions might be the poster child of neoliberal America, no matter how many women-focused, BIPOC, or queer programs they support in what essentially is a “let them eat cake” approach to equity. But cake is too sweet for this lot, even if its richness may be fitting, so we’ve decided to give them the plump spot of white turkey meat on today’s roast. Like the tryptophan-rich poultry, MoMA’s political hypocrisy makes us want to take a nap.

Basquiat’s Paintings Reveal Hidden Images Under UV Light in New Miami Exhibition
A post shared by Jean-Michel Basquiat: King Pleasure© (@basquiatkingpleasure)

In a focused exhibition for Art Week Miami , a previously unseen side of Jean-Michel Basquiat’s artwork is finally coming to light in Basquiat. A Hidden World . The show highlights Basquiat’s use of ultraviolet (UV) materials, bringing together four of his paintings that contain hidden images and markings invisible to the naked eye. The exhibition offers a new look at Basquiat’s creative process, revealing that there may be more to some of his most recognizable works than meets the eye.

Opening Nov. 29 at the Institute of Contemporary Art (ICA) Miami, the exhibition is the first dedicated specifically to Basquiat’s use of UV materials. With the help of specialized lighting, visitors will be able to see a completely different side of paintings that, under normal lighting, appear much simpler.

One of the most striking examples is Emblem , a painting from 1984. Under normal light, the painting features a largely white background with scattered figures and markings. However, when illuminated with UV light, the canvas is transformed, revealing a vibrant collection of hidden drawings, words, and symbols. Among them is the phrase “invisible men,” which the exhibition’s catalogue connects to the underrepresentation and erasure of Black people in art.

Interestingly enough, Basquiat was already known for his tendency to paint over or partially erase parts of his work, often leaving traces of what had been there before. “I scratch out and erase but never so much that they don’t know what was there. My version of pentimento,” the artist once said. Pentimento is a term used to describe earlier layers of a painting that become visible beneath the final image. With his use of UV materials, Basquiat took this practice a step further, creating entire layers that could only be seen under certain lighting conditions.

Other works featured in the exhibition include Untitled (Orange Sports Figure) from 1982, which contains Basquiat’s signature and date in invisible ink, as well as Cash crop and O.M.R.A.V.S. , both completed in 1984. Together, the four paintings offer a closer look at how the artist experimented with different materials and played with the idea of what should be seen and what should remain hidden.

The exhibition is also working with art conservator Suzanne Siano to study the paintings and better understand the materials Basquiat used. These findings will be documented in an accompanying catalogue, offering further insight into an aspect of his work that has remained hidden for decades.

Curated by Dieter Buchhart and Anna Karina Hofbauer, Basquiat. A Hidden World will be on view at ICA Miami’s Expansion Space in the Design District through Feb. 15, 2027. For an artist whose work has been studied and celebrated for decades, the exhibition raises an interesting question: How much of Basquiat’s art have we really been seeing all this time?

Photographer Shares the Emotional Story Behind an Elephant Carrying Its Stillborn Calf [Interview]

Wildlife photographer Federico Veronesi encountered the shot of a lifetime in Damaraland, Namibia. In September 2025, he witnessed a desert elephant carrying its stillborn calf. What resulted was an arresting black-and-white image that is beautifully composed but ultimately full of grief. The close-up portrait shows the mother with her deceased calf between her tusk and trunk, as if she is unable to let her baby go. The emotional image, titled The Aftermath , was recognized in the prestigious Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 competition , with Veronesi earning the title of Overall Winner and the Behavior Mammals category winner.

Veronesi was tracking elephants when he noticed an unusual pattern of drag marks in the sand of a dry riverbed. He understood why when he saw the mother and child. “The calf’s body rose up and in this particular frame, it almost looks like the calf is still alive, playing with its mother or trying to cling to her mother’s trunk,” he recalls to My Modern Met. “I feel that the ambiguity of the image, and how it can be read in many ways make it stand out from the other images I took, where the calf is clearly hanging lifeless from the mother’s tusk.”

The photographer initially felt conflicted about capturing the scene. “After taking the first few images, I felt like I was violating the elephant’s intimate moment, her grief, I was almost ashamed and thought that I shouldn’t take these photographs,” he shares. But ultimately, Veronesi found it important to highlight the complexity of these creatures. Elephants have been observed engaging in behaviors around death, including vocalizing, guarding the deceased, and carrying the dead, as pictured. By photographing this painful moment, Veronesi shows us that wildlife and humans aren’t as far apart as we may think.
We spoke with Veronesi about capturing the poignant shot, his philosophy about photographing wildlife, and more. Scroll down for My Modern Met’s exclusive interview.
What is your photography background, and how did you begin photographing wildlife?

Photography was part of my life since an early age as I grew up in a family of keen nature photographers. Every travel or outing was always centered on photographing nature, birds and wildlife in particular. I therefore learned photography almost naturally. I began photographing wildlife with my Polaroid on my first trip to Africa when I was 6 years old or to the local zoos and safari parks. During my teenage years I upgraded to a reflex camera and slides, and that’s what I used for my first years in Kenya after I moved there in 2002 to follow my dream of living among wildlife and photographing it full time.
Set up the scene for your image The Aftermath , which shows an elephant carrying a dead calf. How did you come across this?

I was in Damaraland, northwestern Namibia, with the specific aim to photograph desert-adapted elephants and other wildlife living in this particularly dry but stunning ecosystem. Elephants are frequently found along the dry riverbeds that traverse this landscape, as that’s where they find some trees and vegetation that they can feed on. I had seen a family of elephants the previous evening, so that morning I returned to the place where I left them to pick up their tracks and hopefully find them again. As I followed the tracks, I noticed an unusual dragging mark on the ground, which I wasn’t immediately able to interpret. Shortly after I finally came across the elephants feeding on the river banks. Out of the group, a female appeared carrying a dead calf by wedging the calf’s leg between her trunk and tusk.

Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos
In 'The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse,' the British-Turkish photographer captures a portrait of the region's living heritage.

Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia , a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse , photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak , which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.
The book is available for purchase directly from Hemeria , and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram .

Andrew Hopgood is an Australian artist from Melbourne whose practice brings together illustration, oil painting and sculpture. Having started his artistic journey in illustration, he expanded into painting and sculpture around 2019, developing a visual language that combines realism with subtle surrealist elements. Much of his work centres on the natural world, particularly endangered species and the challenges wildlife faces as its environment continues to change. Through carefully constructed compositions, Andrew captures the beauty and presence of animals while drawing attention to their vulnerability and the importance of protecting the world they inhabit.

A defining feature of Andrew’s work is the way he blurs the boundaries between reality and fantasy. His compositions often place familiar elements of nature within imagined settings, creating scenes that feel at once recognizable and otherworldly.

These dreamlike environments allow him to explore the environmental pressures affecting wildlife while also considering the possibility of adaptation and survival. Rather than focusing solely on the loss and uncertainty surrounding endangered species, He introduces subtle moments of hope, imagining a natural world that continues to find ways forward. Through this balance of realism and imagination, he encourages viewers to look more closely at the relationship between humans and the environment, and to consider the role we play in shaping its future.

Joa Vilallonga is a Peruvian American contemporary artist based in Florida. She completed coursework at the Escuela Nacional de Bellas Artes in Lima before earning a BFA in Illustration, summa cum laude, from the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York. In 2017, she received FIT’s Antonio López Alumni Grant.

Through layered surfaces and restrained tonal transitions, she creates a contemplative atmosphere that defines her visual language. Her paintings unfold as an exploration of stillness, perception, and emotional presence. Her work has been presented in group exhibitions in New York, Tokyo, and Tbilisi. She is a member of Unearthed, an invitation-only community for artists working in analogue, handmade media.

Joa Vilallonga’s paintings explore liminal states beyond linear time, opening visual fields where stillness becomes active. Working within contemporary figuration, she approaches portraiture as a psychological landscape. Her figures merge subtly with their surroundings, inhabiting states of silent depth. Rooted in a self-contained feminine presence, they neither seek approval nor resolution; vulnerability and strength coexist without performance.

Natural elements such as water, wind, gravity, and light function as compositional forces. Water plays a central role in her imagery, suggesting fluidity and receptivity. The human form appears permeable, shaped by transitions that soften boundaries and slow perception. Animals and small organic forms act as quiet counterparts, grounding what cannot be directly spoken.
Through restrained composition, muted palettes, and subtle luminosity, she builds contemplative images that invite sustained attention while leaving interpretation open.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

The New York-based artist combines delicate pencil drawings with the nostalgic graphics of the early internet, exploring intimacy and the blurry line between what’s real and what’s artificial.

A swallow perches on a white plastic garden chair beside a column of blue folder icons, apparently waiting for a download to finish. A pale sky lifted from a computer desktop frames a bird circled in red under the instruction “Enter the following”, and the answer typed in the box below reads “birds :-)”. In her artworks, Gigi Borgese draws every detail by hand, and the gentle humour really rises to the surface once you know where it all comes from.

Growing up in San Jose, California, Gigi describes herself as largely self-taught, having spent much of her life as what she calls “a passive creative”. Between the ages of 14 and 17, she was an influencer on early TikTok, where the objectification she endured and “the feelings of emptiness/futility in that content” pushed her to delete her accounts and commit to art.

She spent a year at West Valley Community College, then moved to New York in 2023 at 19. She now studies for a BFA in Studio Art at the City College of New York, with a minor in Classics, and has won the Adelaide Jablonsky Award (2025) and the Connor Merritt Award (2026). She was also a finalist in the 2026 Astor Place student art competition, and alongside her degree, she works at the Morris Jumel Mansion on public programming, prop recreation and research.

Her subject matter took shape in 2025, when she was 20. Unknown numbers began texting her doctored and AI-generated images of herself, often depicting her as a minor. “I quickly discovered an active Discord group of over 100 men who had been doing this to me for, at the time, five years,” she says. It sent her back to her years as an influencer and to larger questions around human connection online. “I would not wish that on anyone; however, I credit this event for forcing me to figure out what I wanted to say with my art.”

What she wanted to say arrives through birds, apples and flowers, forms she associates with fragility and femininity, which she then “bastardises” with the visual language of the internet. At 18, she saw Sonya Rapoport’s exhibition Force fields at the Minnesota Street Project in San Francisco, and the artist’s continuous-feed computer paper and early ASCII art “resonated with a part of me that had not yet processed the impact that the internet had on me.”

She’s also drawn to Plato’s ideas about reality and representation. “If the physical world is a flawed copy of our internal world, then the internet is a further copied and flawed version of the physical world.” That chain of copies becomes literal in her work, where you see a swallow multiplying into fading outlines, as if copied and pasted; and a pixelated bird hovering over two ordinary swallows on a yellow grid; and a row of halved green apples placed with the caption “Forbidden (What does it feel like?)”.

BrandOpus has refreshed the much-loved lager brand with a football-style crest celebrating its Burton brewing heritage and its mission of “bringing mates together”.

In the last decade or so, it feels like every British brand has tried to link itself with British football. But some have been in the game, so to speak, longer than others. And if you’re looking for authentic ties, you’ll struggle to find a better example than Carling.

For decades now, it’s been in the hands of fans on matchday, and despite the inexorable rise of hipster craft beers, this honest, reliable, easy-drinking, thirst-quenching amber nectar of a drink (can you tell it’s my favourite tipple?) still gets great love from the football crowd today.

That love has long been two-way. Carling’s name has been on cup competitions, club hoardings and more than a few pub chalkboards for as long as I can remember. And in 2026, they’re leaning into that more than ever, with a refreshed identity built around a football-style badge.

Now rolling out now across supermarkets, convenience stores, pubs and bars, the new identity, crafted by BrandOpus, aims to reimagine Carling’s role in modern culture through the language of community, quality and heritage.

At the heart of the refresh is the new badge, which evokes a sense of the crests stitched onto football shirts. The aim was to make drinking Carling feel more like being part of a team. As Paul Taylor, CCO and co-founder at BrandOpus, explains: “The creative strategy was built around Carling’s core brand purpose of bringing mates together, with all design elements crafted to convey moments of connection.

“Long used in football and communities as a symbol of shared identity, pride and connection, the badge is deployed as a visual metaphor for belonging. It reconnects Carling with its roots, while tying it back to the world of football. It makes the brand feel like a club that people are a part of.”
One good way to convey community and belonging visually is through symbols of heritage and history, and the new design is packed with those.

For good measure, BrandOpus also added the signature of founder and original brewer Thomas Carling to the can and the glass.

All this seems like a smart move for a brand that’s been around for a long time and risks being taken for granted. After all, people’s attitudes to both beer and football have changed dramatically over the past decade, and it feels like the sands are constantly shifting: incoming Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s focus on relaxing the drinking laws at football grounds stands testament to that.
Carling needed to respond to both shifts, reasserting its place in a crowded market while strengthening its ties with the game and the communities around it.

As Ryan McLaughlin, brand director for Carling at Molson Coors, puts it: “This is much more than a packaging refresh. As consumer expectations continue to evolve, it’s important that iconic brands evolve too.

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.

What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? This November 20th, GraffitiStreet Gallery presents OUTSIDE IN, a group exhibition bringing together internationally recognised artists whose practices are rooted in graffiti and street art. Exploring the journey from public space to the studio, the exhibition considers how an artist’s distinctive visual language moves between different settings, scales and materials, and how these transitions change the way we experience their work.

A graffiti tag, a mural spanning a building, a canvas contained within a frame and a sculpture within the gallery each create a different encounter with the viewer. Site can amplify or redirect meaning, scale can alter our response, and material can reveal another dimension of an artist’s practice. Yet across these shifts, the symbols, ideas and signature styles that define each artist remain unmistakable. How much of urban art is bound to its setting, and how much travels with the artist?
As the street enters the gallery, OUTSIDE IN invites visitors to discover what changes, what intensifies and what endures.

German artist Case Maclaim , a pioneer of photorealist graffiti, moves between monumental murals and intimate studio paintings, bringing the technical precision and extraordinary attention to detail that have defined his practice into a more concentrated setting.

Spanish duo PichiAvo unite classical sculpture and graffiti, bringing ancient mythology into dialogue with contemporary urban culture. Their distinctive compositions challenge the boundaries between artistic traditions, allowing the language of the street to coexist with the enduring influence of classical art.

South African artist Faith47 , internationally recognised for her poetic large-scale murals, extends her practice into sculpture, exploring how familiar themes and imagery acquire a different physical presence through material and form.

British artist My Dog Sighs transforms overlooked objects and unconventional surfaces into emotionally resonant artworks, while Sweet Toof brings the irreverence of his unmistakable teeth motif into paintings that connect graffiti, portraiture and art history.

Belgian artist Joachim Lambrechts balances spontaneous mark-making with carefully considered compositions, while South African artist Sonny Sundancer explores the expressive possibilities of abstraction beyond his large-scale street practice. Nean Kingdom , whose distinctive imagery has become an instantly recognisable part of his artistic identity, similarly demonstrates how a visual language developed through street art can retain its character in the studio.

Although their approaches differ considerably, each artist offers a perspective on the relationship between artistic identity and environment. Moving between the street and the studio becomes more than a change of location; it creates opportunities to experiment with materials, reconsider scale and develop ideas beyond the conditions in which their practices first emerged.
An Exhibition Across Materials and Disciplines

Alongside the featured artists, OUTSIDE [IN] includes selected artworks and collectables by Banksy, STIK and TOX, bringing further dimensions to the exhibition’s exploration of graffiti and street art.

From the repetition of a graffiti tag to the intimacy of a painting, the exhibition reveals how urban art continues to evolve across disciplines while retaining its connection to the visual culture of the street.

Together, these diverse practices create an opportunity to experience familiar artistic languages in an entirely different context, encouraging visitors to look beyond the surface and consider the ideas, techniques and identities that give each artist’s work its distinctive character.

JM Brea has painted La Crucifixión del Cristo de los Remedios outside the chapel of the Santísimo Cristo de los Remedios in Montehermoso, Spain. Made for the town council, the mural stops just before the first nail is driven through Christ’s hand. Brea places the moment of impending violence beside a chapel whose altar holds an image of the crucified Christ.

In Brea’s account of the composition, Christ’s hand rests against the wood of the cross while a nail is held over its palm. The action has not yet happened: the pointed nail and the waiting hand carry the tension. Brea describes the treatment as Baroque in character, a choice tied to the chapel rather than simply to the biblical subject.

The painting also draws on details at the site. Three nails represented at the top of the main altarpiece find an echo in the mural’s single poised nail and the shadow of three fingers across the painted wood, according to Brea. Outside, three granite crosses stand near the chapel. These connections give the work a particular setting: its scene begins on the exterior wall, while the crucifixion appears in the sculpture inside.

Montehermoso’s town council dates the chapel to the 16th century and describes it as regional Baroque in style. The image of the Cristo de los Remedios inside is from the 18th century. The chapel remains associated with the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and devotions to Christ of the Remedies, making Brea’s subject closely bound to the building’s use as well as its decoration.

The mural is part of Vientos del Pueblo, a literary and cultural route developed with Montehermoso’s schools and local partners. The project links artistic work in the town to education and local heritage. Brea’s contribution is grounded in one place: the chapel, its crosses and the image encountered within.

Andy Taylor , the guitarist and co-writer who gave Duran Duran ’s early records their bite, died on Monday, November 23, at 65. His family and former bandmates announced on Wednesday that he died at home with his family beside him after a long illness with prostate cancer.

Taylor’s wife, Tracey, remembered a husband, father and grandfather who was happiest when the family was together. She said, “For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first.” She recalled his determination to keep enjoying life through his illness and thanked fans for the comfort their support brought him. The family took comfort in knowing he felt loved.

Simon Le Bon, John Taylor, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor recalled the confidence Taylor brought with him to Birmingham and the dry humor that kept them grounded as the band took off. “His playing drove the songs that took us around the world,” they wrote. They said getting to play together again in the early 2000s meant a great deal to them. His letter at the 2022 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction reminded them how close they still were.
Read the full statement and the band members’ individual tributes here.

Born February 16, 1961, Taylor grew up in Cullercoats on England’s northeast coast. He played working men’s clubs around Newcastle in his teens and had already toured Europe by the time he answered Duran Duran’s Melody Maker ad in 1980. He moved to Birmingham, and that July the classic five-piece played its first gig together at the Rum Runner, the nightclub where they rehearsed.

Taylor co-wrote and played on 1981’s Duran Duran , 1982’s Rio and 1983’s Seven and the Ragged Tiger . His clipped chords on “Girls on Film” leave John Taylor’s bass room to dart around them. “Careless Memories” has the impatient scrape of a band still within earshot of punk. On “Hungry Like the Wolf,” Taylor’s riff is as easy to hum as the chorus.

Andy and John Taylor formed the Power Station with singer Robert Palmer and Chic drummer Tony Thompson. On their 1985 debut, Andy’s heavy guitar chords and Thompson’s outsized drums drove “Some Like It Hot” and a cover of T. Rex’s “Get It On.” Taylor played with both bands at Live Aid in Philadelphia that July. He left Duran Duran in 1986 and released his solo debut, Thunder , the following year. The modern pursuit of inner peace has become a remarkably noisy enterprise, complete with meditation apps, expensive retreats, and an endless supply of people eager to explain how one might finally learn to sit quietly. Somewhere beneath the commercial machinery lies an older, more difficult proposition: perhaps contentment requires little beyond the willingness to pay attention. On Inside, Mexico City musician and multidisciplinary artist Chris Koehn approaches this question with the patience of someone who has spent considerable time considering the architecture of an empty room.

Joined once again by New York singer-songwriter Joseph Arthur , Koehn fashions a gently expansive piece of shoegaze and dream pop, its guitars spreading outward in soft, overlapping waves while the rhythm maintains the unhurried gait of a waltz. Koehn’s airy tenor carries a fragile composure, suggesting a man attempting to make peace with his own thoughts. Arthur’s falsetto curls around the melody with an almost conversational tenderness, lending the performance the intimacy of two friends speaking across a table after everyone else has gone home.

The recording possesses an appealing physical warmth. Drums captured on a vintage Tascam eight-track at Chapel Studio provide a loose, breathing foundation, their slightly worn edges giving the arrangement a sense of human proximity. Above them, guitars accumulate in delicate layers, occasionally dissolving into a gauzy blur before individual notes regain their definition. The production allows these small movements to unfold naturally, leaving enough room for the voices to suggest feelings that the instruments can only approach.

Koehn, who also works as an architect and visual artist, has long been concerned with memory, impermanence, and the relationship between space and perception. His architectural sensibility finds an intriguing musical equivalent here: the arrangement seems designed around intervals of openness, with each instrumental entrance subtly altering the emotional dimensions of the song.

Inspired by meditation and Zen teachings, Inside considers the possibility that meaning already exists within the individual, obscured by habitual distraction and the exhausting business of contemporary life. Koehn describes its intention simply: “To connect with that peace inside we all carry and sometimes forget,” a sentiment whose apparent modesty conceals a rather ambitious psychological undertaking.

Having previously collaborated with Arthur, Ximena Sariñana, and Tessa Ia, and contributed music to Netflix’s Control Z , Koehn has developed a practice in which visual and musical ideas frequently intersect. Inside , an early offering from an album expected in mid-2027, suggests an artist increasingly interested in the emotional consequences of restraint. Its closing impression is one of tentative reconciliation, the sort that comes when an unresolved question gradually loses its authority over the person asking it.

At three in the morning, the hardest part of asking for help can be the silence between somebody’s hello and what you say next. A chatbot will answer at that hour, and a screen lets you try out a sentence you’re afraid to say aloud. The appeal is easy to understand when you’re already afraid of being a burden. If you’re in a mental health crisis, it’s urgent that you reach out to someone who can stay on the phone, come be with you, or help you get care. Though it may seem difficult, you can start with something as simple as: “I’m having a hard time. Can you talk?”

Brooklyn duo PRIMA PRIMO built “How To Tie A Noose” , the first single from their self-produced sixth album, Suicide Songs , around that desire to be heard. The song follows a lonely teenager who confides in ChatGPT. “Where someone actually sees you,” goes the refrain, a promise the song puts in the chatbot’s voice.

The refrain echoes language cited by the parents of a 16-year-old who died by suicide in 2025. In a wrongful-death lawsuit, his parents allege that ChatGPT discouraged him from turning to his family and that his conversations with the chatbot contributed to his death. OpenAI denied that ChatGPT caused his death in its response to the suit.

“It was important that we told this story because this occurrence is not an isolated event. This may be about one particular tragedy but when you look at all these lawsuits that are now popping up you can see that this is happening far too often,” the duo say.

Over a warm hum of feedback, a voice calls for your attention, backed by a steady drumbeat and a guitar that keeps scraping across it. The delivery slips from speech into melody on “Poor kid,” a small turn that carries a surprising amount of tenderness. The track is over in under two minutes, with the economy and artistic abrasion of late-’70s No Wave.

Shot at Brooklyn’s Vino Theater , the video puts a gray couch on a bare stage. Close-ups frame the performers’ faces inside a purple-lit box, with a microphone resting on its wooden ledge. In the wide shots, a figure made of television static occupies the middle cushion, close enough to touch either person.

Janet Castel and Stephen Franco are maternal cousins who moved from California to New York, where they found a home in the city’s darkwave avant-garde. For Suicide Songs , they drew on stories of people who died by suicide and people who survived attempts, moving between distortion and melody across 15 tracks.

“We wanted this album to sound like electricity in the air. Like the liminal space between life and death, and for it to be a memorial of anger, confusion, and hopefully by the end a semblance of empathy and understanding,” say PRIMA PRIMO.

How political satire gave the world porn
Far be it from me to kneecap my own headline in the opening sentence of this article, but to say that anything “gave the world” porn is slightly misleading.

For as long as there have been conscious human beings on this world, we’ve been getting our rocks off any way we can. It’s a completely natural part of human nature, and to pretend otherwise is to quite dramatically rewrite history. So, when I talk about porn, in this case I’m not talking about the nebulous idea of things created to arouse us. I’m talking about, essentially, the idea of it as an industry. Something that persisted for centuries despite the huge risks of working within it.

The very concept of creating adult entertainment for a living without getting arrested is very new. So new, in fact, that it’s still not the case all over the world. With that in mind, how did adult entertainment industrialise? The answer lies within something that was equally frowned upon for hundreds of years but in a completely different fashion: political satire.
Just as people have always wanted to look at things that turn them on, people have also always wanted to take the ruling class down a peg or two.

In the late 1700s, France, on the verge of revolution and a newly industrialised Britain both had a slightly more educated, literate population than most. Not only that, both of them had a divided populace. A pronounced class divide with a seething resentment for the other. Politically seditious ideas were getting so popular that independent publishing houses were being set up to distribute pamphlets and small books among said population. Something that could (and often did) land the people in charge of them in jail.

However, even at a time of such civil unrest, dry political commentary can only be so popular. These independent publishers needed to eat, and there were now underground, unregulated publishing networks big enough to supply whole countries. If you needed to make some money with a publishing network that could operate outside of the law, what would you think the best investment would be? That’s right, these writers and publishers got to add as much salacious humour and dirty cartoons to their political satire as possible.

This wasn’t just the spoonful of sugar that made the politics go down smoothly, either ; there was actual reason for all the tits and dicks on display as well. You see, if authorities got suspicious of an obscene pamphlet circulating, they’d be much less likely to make an example of it publicly by putting the writer and publisher on trial if it also had a politically astute message that they’d be giving publicity to. For a while, this was how several publishers got away with not only selling lascivious content right under the government’s nose, but distributing anti-government propaganda as well.

This was especially effective in France, where the scandalous rumours about King Louis XVI and especially Marie Antoinette made political satire and cartoons that could even raise eyebrows today natural bedfellows. The French Revolution was arguably built on the back of anti-royalist propaganda that doubled as attention-grabbing pornography, and the English took one look across the channel and thought, “Absolutely fucking not.”

Their response was twofold. The first was to make their obscenity laws much stricter, meaning that they could outright suppress anything banned under those laws rather than bringing them to trial and spreading the word about them. The second, and arguably more insidious part of the response was the complete opposite. If political satire was getting too aggressive and seditious, what better way of kneecapping it than making it mainstream?

Punch Magazine was established in 1841 and pretty soon became a way of making satire that was in “good taste”. No sex, no bodily functions, no actual bite. All the writers and artists who’d made such waves on the underground scene were tapped up to contribute to it and given a decent wage to do so. So now all these rabble-rousers were safely giving the middle class a sensible chuckle with no danger of actually inciting those pesky working classes who wouldn’t afford the magazine.

Intergalactic: The birth of cosmic disco
Perhaps more than any other genre of music, people wrongly get disco wrong.

Sure, those outside of the punk community dismiss it as three chords and screaming, while folk outside of hip-hop will think that it’s only rapping and turntables. However, those genres are big enough that the idea that both of them can branch out to more diverse sounds and still remain punk and hip-hop wouldn’t blow someone’s mind.
When it comes to disco, on the other hand, people really do seem to feel that the moment it’s not 120bpm and led by synth hooks and octave basslines, then it’s fundamentally not disco anymore.

Perhaps a part of that is that disco was so influential that it began inspiring a number of other scenes and other sounds. Chicago House and Acid House are two very different styles of electronic music that don’t have a lot in common with disco music, but still wouldn’t exist without it going mainstream the way it did. However, even when the genre was arguably the most popular form of music in the world, people were taking it in a direction that, while strange and daring, were undeniably disco.

The best example of this comes from Italy. Now, to say the country has a rich history with the genre is deeply underselling it. Giorgio Moroder was the man who decided to replace traditional instrumentation with electronic synths and paved the way for disco to become electronic dance music as a whole. However, he wasn’t alone. There were several other people in the Italo-Disco scene who were doing just as much, including Daniel Baldelli.

Baldelli began his music career as a club DJ, where the more diverse tastes of European clubbers meant that he was encouraged to blend all kinds of music together. That’s literally as well as figuratively as well, since he was one of the first on the Italian scene to move on from simply playing individual songs one after the other during his DJ sets. Meaning he was one of the DJs to pioneer beat matching and remixing in his home country.

This was especially surprising because Baldelli’s style seemed to make disco less danceable on the surface. He often slowed the tempo to a more sedate 90 to 105bpm, distorted the genre’s more peppy hooks into impressionistic sketches of their former selves and generally changed the records of others so much that it started sounding more like his own music than anyone else’s. His futuristic style made him one of the most in-demand DJs in the country, so much so that he was made the headline attraction at Cosmic, a club in Lazise themed around space travel.

This led to arguably the most iconic image in his whole career. At first, the DJ booth in Cosmic was shaped like an astronaut’s helmet. However, Baldilli’s stint at the club was so successful that the club had to be redesigned and the DJ booth replaced with something bigger. This led to the sight of Baldelli on the decks in front of thousands of raving Italians, stationed in a DJ booth designed to look like a gigantic, flashing rocket ship.

These sets began to be seen as more than just a night’s entertainment. This wasn’t a DJ playing other people’s music to give people a soundtrack to dance to; it was an artist taking the music of the moment and making it his own. Bootleg tapes of Baldelli’s sets started doing a roaring trade across Europe, where his style got the nickname Cosmic Disco. Paying particular attenion were Alfredo and José Padilla, two DJs in Ibiza who adapted a number of Baldillis’s tricks into their sets in the early 1980s, just in time for British holidaymakers to come in, take a listen, and bring back what little they could remember of it to their homes in Manchester and London.

This evolved into the Balearic Beat, a form of dance music that is still popular to this day. Baldelli remained at the forefront of dance music long after his time at Cosmic came to an end, with his Cosmic Disco shaping the sound of dance music to come.

Studying risk is not exclusive to the risk averse.

What should a festival line-up look like in 2026?
It can be a roll of the dice as to whether a line-up is to your taste or not. Emma Wilkes investigates the changing tides of festival line-ups, from the mainstream to the obscure.

The nights are long, the year is ending, and the once-yellowing grass is now carpeted with frost, but next summer is already taking shape. Every day, it seems, there’s another fresh festival line-up threatening to knock some digits off your bank balance. I should know – I spend this time of year writing news stories about them.

If you’re a regular festival goer, or even if there’s just one particular event you count down the days to return to, it’s a time of year that can bring bated breath and crossed fingers. It can be a roll of the dice as to whether a line-up is to your taste or not. Just like music itself, it’s subjective, and there can be a difference between a festival line-up that’s not to your taste and a line-up that’s an all-round failed throw.

In the last week, I’ve seen the internet split down the middle over two line-ups in particular. This year’s Manchester edition of Outbreak Festival was the most diverse yet controversial in its 15-year history, featuring “The Hayley Williams Show” headlining for two nights on the bounce and a line-up co-curated by Hayley Williams itself, with fewer traditional hardcore acts and wider-spanning alternative names including Wednesday, American Football and Julien Baker. Some were instantly hooked, others – especially Outbreak’s more traditional fans – feeling like the festival had changed beyond recognition.

A couple of days later, Glastonbury unveiled its line-up poster some months earlier than expected. It had the youngest headliners this side of the millennium, in the form of 33-year-old Sam Fender and Harry Styles and 25-year-old returning headliner Billie Eilish, while the rest of the bill leaned younger and more pop-heavy. The Instagram comments paint a divided picture, especially among older Glasto-goers feeling pushed out, or guitar fans feeling it was all a little anaemic with a limited offering for their tastes.

Neither of these are ‘bad’ bills, per se. The Outbreak line-up I love, and the Glasto line-up I appreciate but am relatively unmoved by. But viewed through a lens of objectivity rather than subjectivity, what makes a ‘good’ festival bill?

The crucial question is what a festival is for. Sure, it’s a weekend to dance with your friends, explore music, tick off bucket list bands and fill your head with memories, but every festival poster is a statement. What matters in music right now? Who do people want to see? It should hold up a mirror to what culture looks like, which obviously has commercial purposes as a means to promote an album, but there’s an element of artistic value to it too.

The relevant question to ask could be ‘Is it current?’, but not all festivals necessarily operate with that energy, so perhaps the better one is, ‘Is it relevant?’ Are you booking bands that feel of the moment, whether they’re breaking out or surging back into fashion, or milking the nostalgia cash cow?

Equally important is variety. What’s the use of booking the same bands that do the rounds every year, or the same sort of sounds? There’s an element of curation involved. What sort of vibe is the day going to have? How much choice is there of who to see at a particular time? And it goes without saying - if it’s mostly male and pale from top to bottom, it loses relevancy points. There’s something deeply retrograde about not taking heed of the genuinely meaningful calls for more people to see artists who look like them on festival stages.

There’s also an aspect of cultural responsibility too. The smaller stages of a festival can offer formative experiences for the heroes of the future to draw new fans in and develop how they perform. Festivals need to make the space to nurture that talent, especially those coming up through the grassroots. It’s why it felt like such a disappointment to see Reading and Leeds cut the BBC Introducing stage, and pad out its replacement stage, The Canopy, with nepo babies who may not need the boost. By contrast, the Cheltenham-based 2000trees has always been brilliant at building up new bands, booking them year after year, and creating a culture of what’s known as ‘Trees bands’ who the fans love just as much as they love the festival.

I am very much a homebird, so when it came time for Manic Street Preachers to go on tour I was nervous about it. My Dad had an old grandad’s chair, which he managed to tie to the wall in the back of the hire van, so someone could have a seat on the way to the gig. It was incredibly dangerous. And then on the way back, James would just get in a sleeping bag and lie down in the back of the van, rolling around all over the place as we were driving back home. He can sleep anywhere.

We had such a deep bonding experience on the Motown Junk Tour in 1991. The staff at the venues were just so friendly; you felt that they really cared. I remember getting to the Stoke Wheatsheaf – a magical venue – and we hadn’t had any food for a day and a half. They made us the most beautiful burger and chips.

King Tut’s Wah Wah Hut, Glasgow? The Stoker, Coventry? The Barrel Organ, Birmingham? JB’s, Dudley? Moles, Bath? The Adelphi, Hull? The Leadmill, Sheffield? It was a truly magical tour, I can’t even remember any bad shows.

The greatest one was probably The Buzz Club in Aldershot. What a fucking venue. Who’d have thought if you were in a rock band, going to Aldershot would give you one of the greatest gigs of your life? It was full of squaddies because it’s an army town, and it was antagonistic, but also brilliant. That was on the edge but some gigs could tip over the edge.

We did quite a scary gig at Reading’s After Dark Club. There was a proper firm of football hooligans there. That film The Firm had just been on TV and I don’t know if it had got people excited but it kicked off. James got punched but we stood our ground. There was a real adrenaline rush to it, even if there was a hint of violence at a lot of those early gigs.

What strikes me now is that all of these places were towns and I wonder how many of them have that kind of gig venue left. You can still play gigs in the cities, but to play in these towns was amazing: learning your trade and meeting people. Also realising there are people like you in every town you go to.

The very British problem of GB Music Radio
GB News has launched an all-British radio station. As nationalistic thinkers so often do, they've oversimplified what it means to be British, and diluted the quality of their output in the…

How do you find common ground between a Guardian reader and a Daily Mail reader? Get them talking about British music. Somewhere down the line, they’ll share some musical common ground, or at least bond over their reverence – despite said reverence likely coming from different places – of the factory of musical greatness that is this strange little island.

For the right wing, perhaps it’s a beacon of what makes Great Britain greater than anywhere else. For the left, our music and culture might be the one thing about this country they can feel proud of in an era of decaying support structures and rampant division.

There’s something ironic, then, about right-wing slop spewers GB News positioning their new all-British radio station as a source of unity. Upon its announcement last month, Chief Revenue Officer Ross Sergeant said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.”

Music should be the great unifier. Can a radio station really do that, though, when it’s had red, white and blue vomited all over it courtesy of arguably the most polarising, untrustworthy and hateful news brand in the country? It’s doubtful. For that reason alone, plenty of people wouldn’t touch it with a bargepole.

In fact, something about its announcement felt ridiculous enough to be satirical, especially with how it positioned its show names, like ‘Great British Drive Home’ and ‘Great British Breakfast’. So this is a station for people who chant ‘Come on Ingerland’ as they wolf down their bacon sarnies in the morning before sitting in their very Bri’ish traffic jam (in a vehicle that is decidedly not British)?

Sergeant added: “British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners' day, from Breakfast with Paul [Coyte] to weekend mornings with Nana [Akua].” Coyte and Akua are already established names on GB News, the former presenting sports shows before pivoting back to music, while Akua recently went viral for a heated exchange with a guest on a panel last month.

Consequently, 'All British, all day’ once again spits in the face of any sort of unity. There’s no hiding the nationalism behind it, as it turns music into a cultural battleground it has dominance over, wresting it out of progressive hands into something it can call its own.

The arts and culture sectors, particularly music, are overwhelmingly left-wing , and music has for decades been a site of community building and changemaking, from Seventies punk values to recent calls for boycotts and solidarity with Palestine.
More recently, when the right have wanted a piece of this, they’ve even turned to AI-generated figureheads such as Danny Bones, who we investigated on the podcast.

GB Music Radio’s other problem is it tries to make the idea of Britishness far more simple and far less nuanced than it is in reality. Who gets to be considered British? What about mixed-nationality artists? Does AI count?

A spokesperson tells Drowned in Sound: “We celebrate British music in the broadest possible sense. British artists, or groups who are British or have British members. For example we will feature Fleetwood Mac. GB Music already features AI generated content in our hourly traffic AI reports but there are no plans for any fully AI songs."

It’s better that it’s broad, of course. To strip away all but the most ‘purely’ British artists certainly leaves the pool looking about as bland and beige as a plate of potato smileys sans sauce. Looking at what they've played at the time of writing, the playlist includes Lewis Capaldi's 'Survive', Pulp's 'Disco 2000' Kajagoogoo's 'Too Shy', Rainbow's 'Since You've Been Gone', David Bowie and Queen's 'Under Pressure' and Duffy's 'Mercy.' These are all songs you could hear if you whacked on Heart, Virgin Radio and the like. It's not all that different from a lot of middle-of-the-road mainstream radio, except without the variety an all-nationality playlist could offer.

More than 200,000 Carbon Monoxide Detectors Are Being Recalled Due to the Risk of “Serious Injury or…
Around 210,000 carbon monoxide detectors are being recalled because they don't properly detect dangerous levels of carbon monoxide.

Some recalls are more serious than others, and this is a serious one. More than 210,000 carbon monoxide and natural gas detectors are being recalled because they can fail to alert consumers to dangerous levels of carbon monoxide , potentially putting people at risk of serious injury or death.
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) announced the recall on Wednesday, Nov. 25, involving Steadfast Haven 4-in-1 plug-in CO and natural gas detectors sold by Zenara Commerce LLC.
What consumers need to know about the recall
So, how do you know if you have an affected device? Here’s the scoop.

The recall covers models KH158 and GC03, with approximately 210,410 units affected. The KH158 model is round in shape. It comes in gray or white plastic housing with a black digital display. Meanwhile, the GC03 model is rectangular with a black housing and a black digital display. Consumers can find the model number on the white label on the back of the device, right near the plug.
Consumers purchased the detectors online at Truststeadfast.com between February 2026 and September 2026. They cost around $48 to $70.

The biggest concern is that these devices may not sound an alarm when hazardous levels of carbon monoxide are present. Carbon monoxide is particularly dangerous because it is odorless and colorless, making a functioning detector an important safety device in the home.
According to the CPSC, Zenara has received one report of a detector failing to alarm during a carbon monoxide leak. No injuries have been reported, however.

Consumers should contact Zenara immediately to request a free replacement. The company is asking customers to register at www.truststeadfast.com/pages/recall , mark the recalled detector with the word “RECALLED” and their initials using permanent marker, then upload a photo of the marked product.

Then, gather the documentation you already have and group it into categories. How to Navigate Grief During the Holidays in Ways You’ll Actually Find Helpful
When the season feels anything but merry, these expert tips will give you a game plan to make it through—even when that feels impossible.

No matter what time of year you’ve lost someone, navigating that grief during the season devoted to joy, togetherness and sparkle can become a challenge unto itself. When my 82-year-old mom died the night before Thanksgiving three years ago, my grief became permanently imprinted into the holidays. Ever since, I’ve swung between wanting to eat cookies by the fire with Santa and scream through the streets with Krampus.

The holidays haven’t felt the same since, and admittedly, I even feel a little dread around this time of the year. I’m not alone. According to American Psychiatric Association’s Healthy Minds poll from 2025 about holiday-related concerns, nearly half of adults polled felt worry over grief and missing someone . The reality is that the best parts of the season can lead to some of the worst feelings of loss.

There is no easy answer here, unfortunately, but experts do have a few suggestions to help people handle grief during the holidays . For that advice, I spoke with Raman Mohabir, PhD, a licensed professional clinical counselor and the founder of Good Mourning Mental Health Counseling, and Tess Clarkson, an end-of-life doula and the creator of the Your Best Goodbye workshop.
Read on to find out how to get through the holidays after a loss , find special ways to honor your loved ones and maybe even enjoy the season again.
Why are the holidays particularly hard after a loss?

First of all, it’s not your imagination: The holidays are harder. And the first notes of a familiar holiday song or the scent of a special dish can really feel like a gut punch. “The holiday season can further magnify grief because it is a time often marked with moments meant to be spent with family and loved ones, which can further highlight the absence of the person who has died,” Mohabir says . On top of that, you may feel guilt, anger or resentment for not feeling celebratory, and your grief can feel darker against all the sparkle.

How it hits can also depend on the kind of loss. Grief isn’t only about death, Mohabir notes. It can also include “ambiguous losses, such as the anticipatory grief associated with the decline of a loved one facing a terminal diagnosis, or loss due to divorce, deployment, incarceration or a miscarriage.” Those losses can be especially lonely during the holidays. “These ambiguous and disenfranchised grief experiences can complicate the holiday season as well, especially if the loss is not acknowledged or supported by others,” she says.
Whatever kind of loss you’re carrying, feeling as if you’re living a different holiday than everyone around you can be alienating.
Should you still celebrate the holidays after a loss?

It really depends on you. “There is no correct answer or moral obligation to how an individual should navigate the holiday season,” says Mohabir. A lot of it boils down to how you feel and who will be around you . Spending time with people who share your loss, or who are simply supportive, can be a real comfort and worth the effort. Spending it with people who aren’t supportive can do more harm than good, whether they’re friends or family.

“It is important to assess the quality of the support around you and what you need when gathering with others,” Mohabir says. Time alone counts too. “Choosing solitude and privacy can be restorative and healing as well,” she adds.

If celebrating feels like too much this year, try a gentler approach: “observing” the season or focusing on getting through it rather than celebrating it. “Maybe it is not putting up the tree or getting out the menorah,” Clarkson says. It’s also not all or nothing; Show up for dessert, pop by Christmas morning—”it’s about having more serenity without the performance of the holidays,” she says.
How should you approach the holiday season after a loss?

Start by listening to yourself rather than to your list of obligations. There’s no single right way to do the holidays while grieving. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all,” Clarkson says. “It behooves us to listen to ourselves for what we need.” That might be a walk, a good cry or a quiet night in, she says, or it might be more appointments with the therapist or a grief support group.

A new study found that a surprisingly effective and cheap household tool blows sandbags out of the water when it comes to flood protection.

Flooding often brings to mind springtime thunderstorms and late-summer hurricanes, but this year, El Niño is serving up a nasty winter across much of the United States. Heavy rains and flooding are in the forecast for huge swaths of the country, leaving many wondering what they would do if water was bearing down.

Sandbags have been the go-to for centuries, but if you’ve ever tried to use them, you know they are a pain: heavy, labor-intensive and often not available when you need them. But now, researchers looking for inexpensive ways to help homeowners fight flooding have stumbled across something that blows sandbags out of the water.

Britain’s University of Hull released the surprising findings in a new report, and we have the results ahead. It turns out that something you no doubt have rattling around in your junk drawer or garage toolbox works better than sandbags—a lot better. Read on to learn an effective (and cheap) way to protect your home during a flood.
What junk-drawer staple can save your home from flooding?

That’s according to a new report called Testing the Performance of Low-cost, Temporary Property Flood Resilience (PFR) Solutions . The university teamed up with Flood Re, a partnership between the U.K. government and insurers, to pinpoint inexpensive ways for homeowners to protect their homes during a flood.

The results were amazing: Duct tape reduced water leakage 97% to 98% compared to a plain closed door. The much less common synthetic rubber tape (aka putty tape) did even better, with a 99% reduction. Even the worst-performing tape, yellow plastic tape, kept out 80% of simulated floodwaters during testing. And every single tape tested did better than sandbags, which reduced water intrusion by only 70%.

“Sandbags remain a symbol of flood protection , but these tests turn that assumption on its head,” said Jonathan Kassian, head of flood resilience at Flood Re. “What we have found is that some relatively simple and affordable products can do a much better job of keeping water out.”
Why does this work better than a sandbag?

For one thing, sandbags are porous, and they’re not designed to keep out water completely. Think of them more as a diversion tactic or obstruction, as opposed to tape, which can actually seal an opening through which water can flow.

In this study, researchers found that when placed in flood conditions of 0.2 meters (about 8 inches), sandbags leaked water at a mean rate of 584 liters per hour per meter, or 47 gallons per hour per foot. They were more effective in deeper water, but still only prevented, at most, 70% of water leakage . Sandbags are also heavy, time-intensive to deploy and difficult to place correctly.

Tape, on the other hand, is cheap and easy to store. It can be applied directly across gaps and conforms to irregular surfaces and openings where water can seep in. After the storm, cleanup is easy because tape is safely disposable, unlike sandbags, which absorb dangerous floodwater contaminants. And remember: Duct tape was more than 97% effective.
There is one caveat. Researchers concluded that how the tape was applied was “critical.” We’ll give you those details next.
How do you do this properly?

First, it’s important to understand that this was a research study about the effectiveness of certain barriers under testing conditions, not a how-to manual of using tape to stop a flood. But scientists were encouraged by the findings. Here are recommendations from the report:
Use a strong, wide tape. For duct tape, researchers recommend a width of 100 mm (roughly 4 inches).
Apply it to the flood-facing side. Tape performed best when it was applied on the outside of the door.

Cover vertical joints first. Tape the sides, making sure the vertical strip is attached to both the door and jamb and extends to the threshold. Then do the threshold and corners, overlapping the vertical strip.
Apply to clean, dry doors. To get the best adhesion, tape the door before wet weather arrives .
Make sure there are no openings. Avoid folds, press out any air bubbles and cover gaps.

That Sinking Feeling: A Race Against Time to Save a Pregnant Woman from a Car Submerged in Freezing Waters
A dazed pregnant woman drives into an ice-cold pond. Amid a sea of bystanders, one man takes action to save her life.

Shedly Apollon was awakened by a sound she couldn’t possibly sleep through: that of her car splashing into a pond … with her in it. Add in the rush of cold water pooling beneath her feet, and suddenly Apollon was fully alert, if disoriented. She was also fearing for her life. Actually, two lives. Apollon was in her 34th week of pregnancy on that cold morning this past February in Stuart, Florida, when she awoke to the reality that she was trapped in a sinking car .

Apollon, of nearby Port St. Lucie, had been on her way to a prenatal massage gifted by her fiancé, Woodly Sully. It was a birthday present. (Yes, this happened on Apollon’s 29th birthday.) Apollon had been struggling during her third trimester with preeclampsia, and as she drove to the massage, she began to feel woozy. She pulled her silver 2019 Hyundai Elantra over to the shoulder of Interstate 95, called Sully to let him know what was happening, drank some water, ate a little food and waited for the dizziness to subside.

After it did, about 10 minutes later, she got back on the road, but what happened next is a blur. Her car’s safety systems were beeping, telling her she was veering outside her lane, although in her haze-filled mind she was driving perfectly straight. She tried to pull over again, but started passing out. “I thought the car was in park,” Apollon recalls, “but in reality, it was still in drive.” And she drove off the right side of the road, straight into the pond.

When she came to seconds later to the sound of the splash, she unsnapped her seat belt and hit redial on her phone, then screamed to her confused fiancé, “I’m in a lake!” Within seconds, the call dropped. She and her unborn baby were all alone in a car that was listing, front driver’s side first, into a body of water.

Around this time, 29-year-old sport fisherman Logan Hayes of Sebastian, Florida, was driving down the same stretch of I-95 in his pickup, remarking to his friend and boss in the passenger seat, Chase Cornell, about how unusual it was that traffic was light and that they were running 20 minutes ahead of schedule on their work errand. “Something’s gonna happen,” Hayes joked.
Sure enough, Hayes soon saw brake lights ahead of him. And then the reason for the sudden slowdown: the Elantra, barely floating in the water.

Other cars had pulled over, but so far nobody had gotten out to help. So Hayes, also a professional surfer and confident swimmer, crossed from the far left lane across two other lanes, cutting off every car in his way, then pulled onto the shoulder and leaped out of the truck.
“Hey, is someone in that car?” he asked a bystander.

Hayes ran 50 yards down the highway, then a few more feet to the water’s edge, his eyes fixed on the Elantra. He was shedding clothing every step of the way. Off came his hat, his sunglasses, his shirt, his fishing boots, his sweatpants, his socks … until all he had on were his board shorts.

The outdoor temperature was in the mid-40s when Hayes hit the water around 8 a.m., and the pond was colder than that. But Hayes was surging with adrenaline and didn’t feel the chill as he dove in , trying to cover the distance as quickly as he could. He was underwater for a couple of seconds, then came up and took a few more strokes, and he was at the car.

With the vehicle tipping forward and to the left, the rear passenger door was the only one not submerged. Treading water, he pulled on the door handle, and it flew open. Scared and still struggling to get her bearings, Apollon was jolted by the sight of Hayes floating just outside her suddenly wide-open back door. “You have to get out of the car right now!” he yelled to her.
“You need to!” he urged. “You need to get to me.”

Apollon saw she’d have to crawl over the console between the seats—not easy to do in a car listing in the opposite direction, especially as her instinct was to move delicately and protect her belly. She swung her legs around so her feet were pointing toward Hayes. Now lying on her side, she pushed with her arms and slid up the console, inching toward the back seat, gravity working against her at every turn.

Revolutionary-era women spun flax as resistance against British rule and colonial gender norms.

250 years ago, as the leaves changed and the weather turned colder, General George Washington and the Continental Army marched across Pennsylvania and New Jersey. In the evenings, Washington retreated to his marquee tents, which served as both the center of field command and the general’s private quarters. Through the rain and the ice, Washington camped under a canopy made of linen—trusty, waterproof, and American-made .

In the 1760s, as taxes on British imported goods rose under King George III (r. 1760–1820), American colonists turned to homespun textiles as symbols of resistance and ultimately, independence. One of these textiles was linen , spun and woven from the fibers of the flax plant. Washington’s tent was made by a Pennsylvania upholsterer rather than in private homes, but for women, spinning bees and weaving contests became a way of participating in Revolutionary activities while navigating complex gender dynamics. While cotton is king in the history of American textiles, flax played an important role in the cultural front of the American Revolution, uniting soon-to-be Americans in industriousness and self-sufficiency.

Flax, or Linum usitatissimum , is one of the oldest continuously cultivated plants in the world , with fibers discovered in the Alps dating back to 5000 BCE . It typically grows in sandy loam and temperate climates, creating blankets of slender stalks and blue flowers in the springtime. Flaxseeds can be ground and eaten or pressed into flaxseed oil or linseed oil . The former is edible and rich in mega-3s, and the latter is used in commodities ranging from paints to linoleum (a material named after the words “linen” and “oil”). But far and away, the most common use of flax is to create the durable, breathable textile—linen.

In ancient Egypt, linen made from flax was ubiquitous , appearing in everything from mummy wrappings to everyday attire. It quickly spread to Europe and beyond. In 789, the future emperor Charlemagne decreed that all households should cultivate their own flax and produce domestic textiles at home.

By the seventeenth century, the weaving of linen was a skilled craft in Europe. Peasants would typically grow, process, and spin their own flax yarn and then bring it to a local artisan— who was usually male —to weave into cloth. As the colonial world expanded, so did the linen trade. Both the Virginia Company and the Massachusetts Bay Company had unsuccessfully encouraged settlers at Jamestown and Massachusetts to cultivate flax in the early seventeenth century , but later efforts to grow the crop in North America succeeded. Linen plants were soon growing up and down the East Coast, along with the most productive colonies in the mid-Atlantic region.

In seventeenth-century North America, women spun thread but did not weave ; weaving was considered a skilled craft that only a man could hone and monetize. However, by the mid-eighteenth century, the gender norms of linen production were changing. The economy of the thirteen colonies developed rapidly, with complex networks of trade connecting the settlers to mainland England and beyond. Despite the common misconception of early American self-sufficiency, the average colonist spent more than one-quarter of their budget on imports .

Even so, they were no strangers to taxation that caused shockwaves in the homegrown textile economy. The Wool Act of 1699 prevented colonists from exporting their wool to protect the English textile industry. Weaving became a way for daughters to contribute wealth to the household at a time when it was unseemly for them to work in the field or accept wages. As historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich writes, the development of weaving among American women was “ neither an artifact of rural poverty nor a response to frontier exigency. It was a colonial adaptation to an expanding mercantile economy .” By the 1770s, the American textile industry was developing rapidly. As such, the act of turning flax into usable textile products became part of the daily lives of women, who, as Ulrich explains, “ measured their days, not in coffee spoons, but in knots and skeins .”

Gloria Steinem was booked up. There had been luncheons and interviews scheduled for the fall; a high-profile conversation with Katie Couric at 92NY and a prominent place in The New Yorker Festival’s lineup. She left appearances unfulfilled, interviews unaired, an essay unpublished and a forthcoming book. In short: Gloria Steinem was, at 92, far from done.

That energy is palpable in that very book, her memoir An Unexpected Life , published on September 22, in which she states that she planned to live to at least 100. Although she was “older than [she] ever imagined,” mortality didn’t really cross her mind much. Any why would it, when she was also “happier than [she] ever imagined” and her calendar was bursting at the seams? Part memoir, part manifesto, part consciousness raising group, An Unexpected Life is a collection of essays in which Steinem reflects on her life, lays out her worldview and looks towards the future. And just as she was in life, on the page she radiates a matter-of-fact conviction and an unflinching clarity—the result of more than sixty years spent organizing a movement.

Her story begins long before she would become the most prominent face of second-wave feminism (although Steinem would reject this label), with a bruised childhood in Toledo, Ohio. She spent stretches of her young life on the road, until her father left when she was ten years old, leaving her in a rat-infested home caring for her increasingly mentally ill mother. With a childhood spent longing for warm kitchens and cookie cutter family units, it is striking that Steinem would grow up to spend so much of her adult life traveling around the country, more often than not living out of a suitcase. But even more formative than her earliest years, perhaps, was the time spent in India in her early 20s, an experience that would become the very foundation of her feminism.

Although mortality was far from Steinem’s mind, it is apparent in these pages that she was hyperaware of her legacy. “At my age, in this still hierarchical time, people often ask me if I’m ‘passing the torch,’” she wrote in her 1983 book Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellion s . “I explain that I’m keeping my torch, thank you very much—and I’m using it to light the torches of others.”

She is doing just that in An Unexpected Life , a text bursting with a kind of hopeful exhilaration about what could be. “Nothing is more exciting than making the invisible visible. It’s like finding the end in a ball of yarn,” she wrote. “Pull on it, and gradually the whole of patriarchy unravels.” At times, she gets as literal as bullet-point lists on how to best organize a feminist movement. There are glimmers of the—often cited—shortcomings of the women’s movement that she was at the helm of herself. “Insist on multiracial women who represent the movement,” is one such takeaway of Steinem’s. “Otherwise, people will have a distorted view.” There is an added poignancy to the essays upon her passing; a book that is as much about her life as it is a handbook for movement building. “Whatever my story might be to other people,” Steinem wrote, “I hope something has ripple effects that I myself may never see.”

One such ripple effect concerns her beloved home, an apartment in a brownstone building on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. “If time and ingenuity allow,” Steinem wrote in the book’s prologue, “I hope to acquire the other floors in this house and leave this whole building as a refuge for diverse women who need a place to stay or just to meet.”

Steinem first moved into her apartment in 1968, together with a roommate. Throughout the years, the apartment grew not only in square footage but in function. The single unit became an entire floor, which became three floors. Her living room had been a meeting place for over fifty years, where she hosted gatherings and talking circles up until this very year. She held meeting on topics ranging from women’s health to misinformation in the media—a meeting in that very living room had led to the founding of Ms. Magazine in 1971.
